blocks.prompt: How a Kite Stays Up
blocks.text: A kite cannot fly on its own. It needs two things. It needs wind, and it needs you. The wind pushes on the flat face of the kite. The string holds the kite back so it cannot blow away. Because the kite leans, the wind slips under it and pushes it up. That push is called lift. The tail helps too. It drags behind and keeps the nose pointed into the wind. A kite with no tail will spin in circles and dive. Let out more string and the kite climbs higher, because the wind blows faster up high, far away from the ground.

blocks.prompt: Older Than the Airplane
blocks.text: Long before anyone built an airplane, people flew kites. The first kites we know about were made in China more than two thousand years ago, out of silk and thin strips of bamboo. Silk is very light and very strong. Bamboo bends a long way before it breaks. Together they made a wing that a person could hold on a string. A kite flies because it leans. Tip a flat sheet into the wind, and the moving air hits the underside and gets pushed downward. Air does not like being shoved, so it shoves back. That push sends the kite up and backward. The string stops the kite from blowing away, so the push has nowhere to go but up. Take the string away and the kite stops flying. It just tumbles off with the wind. The tail is not decoration. It drags along behind and keeps the kite's nose aimed into the wind. A kite without enough tail will spin, roll, and dive into the grass. Here is a strange part. The toy is named after a bird. The red kite is a bird of prey that hangs almost still in a strong wind, and people looked up and saw the same trick.

Angle of attack is the lean into the wind
Too flat means no lift, too steep means a stall
Chinese kite makers worked in silk and bamboo
A kite is a wing on a leash

blocks.prompt: The Four Forces on a String
blocks.text: Every kite in the sky is a small argument between four forces. The wind supplies the first two. When a kite leans into moving air, that air strikes the underside and is deflected downward. Air does not like being shoved, and it shoves back. The part of that push that carries the kite upward is called lift. The part that drives it backward is called drag. Gravity supplies the third force. It pulls straight down on the fabric, the sticks, the tail, and even on the weight of the string itself, which is why a kite cut from a heavy bedsheet will never leave the yard. The fourth force is you. The string does more than stop the kite escaping. It anchors the kite, so the kite cannot simply drift downwind, match the speed of the air, and go limp. Held against the wind, a kite has to either climb or fall, and while the lift beats the weight, it climbs. Let go of the string and all four forces collapse at once. This is why a kite is really a tethered wing. Change how far it leans and you change everything. That lean has a name: the angle of attack. Lean the kite too flat and the air slides past almost untouched, so there is almost no lift. Lean it too steep and drag takes over, the smooth flow breaks up, and the kite stalls and drops. Somewhere between those two failures is the angle that flies. A good kite flier finds it by feel, reading the tug in the line and letting string out or hauling it in. The first people to work this out were kite makers in China more than two thousand years ago, bending split bamboo and stretching silk over it. They had wings on strings for centuries before anyone anywhere wrote down the math of why it worked.

blocks.prompt: The String That Built a Bridge
blocks.text: We hand kites to children, so it is easy to assume that is what they have always been. For most of their history, kites were tools, and serious people used them to do work that nothing else could do. In 1848, engineers wanted to hang a suspension bridge across the Niagara gorge. The problem was obvious and stupid: to build the bridge they needed a cable across the river, and to get a cable across the river they needed a bridge. The water below was far too violent to row. So they held a contest. A teenager named Homan Walsh flew a kite from one rim of the gorge to the other and got his line caught on the far side. That kite string was tied to a slightly heavier cord. The cord pulled across a rope. The rope pulled across a steel cable. The cable carried the bridge. An entire crossing grew out of a piece of string a boy let out into the wind. Fifty years later, kites went to work on the weather. From 1898 the United States Weather Bureau ran a network of kite stations, hoisting recording instruments thousands of feet into the air on piano wire to log temperature, pressure, and humidity. Nobody had ever taken the temperature of the sky day after day before. In 1919, at an observatory in Germany, a train of kites strung along one line reached roughly 9,700 meters, which is higher than most airliners cruise. The kite's most important job came in 1899. Two brothers in Ohio, Wilbur and Orville Wright, built a biplane kite with a wingspan of about five feet. They stood in a field and twisted its wingtips using control lines, watching the kite roll one way, then the other. That was the birth of wing warping, the idea that a flying machine should be steered by reshaping its wings rather than by shifting the pilot's body. Wing warping became the ailerons on every airliner you have ever boarded. The Wrights then flew their first gliders at Kitty Hawk on tethers, as kites, learning the air before they trusted it with their bodies. The kite never really retired. Cargo ships have been towed by computer-steered kites to cut their fuel bills. Kitesurfers cross open water pulled by nothing but a canopy and lines. Engineers are still chasing kites that generate electricity by tugging a tether in loops, high up where the wind is stronger and steadier than any tower can reach. It is a strange kind of demotion. The oldest flying machine on Earth helped invent the newest one, took the temperature of the atmosphere, and started a bridge. Then we put a bow on its tail and gave it to kids.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: The oldest known flying machine, from China over 2,000 years ago
Silk and split bamboo: light, strong, and locally available
Newton's third law does the lifting
1899: the Wright brothers' 5-foot biplane kite
1848: Homan Walsh's kite line started the Niagara bridge

blocks.prompt: The Wing That Is Not Allowed to Leave
blocks.text: Ask most people to name the first flying machine and they will say the airplane. The honest answer is much older, far simpler, and attached to a piece of string. A kite is a wing that is not allowed to leave. That restriction is the whole invention. Throw a free wing into the wind and it does nothing interesting: it travels along with the air, matches its speed, and once it is moving as fast as the air around it there is no flow across its surface and therefore no lift. Tie that same wing to the ground and the air has no choice but to keep rushing past. The kite leans into the stream, the air strikes its underside and is deflected downward, and because every push has an equal push back, the air shoves the kite up and away. Part of that shove is lift, part is drag, and the line absorbs the difference. The tug you feel in your palm is the sky pressing against a shape you made. Kites were flying in China more than two thousand years ago, built from silk stretched over split bamboo. Silk is unreasonably strong for its weight. Bamboo bends a very long way before it breaks. Nowhere else on Earth had that pair of materials so early, which is probably the real reason nowhere else invented the kite first. Good ideas are not distributed evenly, but neither are the materials that let good ideas work. From China the kite spread across Asia and eventually into Europe, where English speakers named it after a bird of prey, the red kite, which hangs almost motionless in a headwind and performs the same trick without a line. For most of its life, the kite was not a toy. In 1848 a teenager named Homan Walsh flew a kite across the Niagara gorge because nobody could get a rope over it. His kite line was tied to a heavier cord, that cord dragged across a rope, the rope hauled across a steel cable, and the cable carried the first suspension bridge over the river. From 1898 the United States Weather Bureau operated kite stations that lifted recording instruments thousands of feet up on piano wire, taking the temperature of the atmosphere day after day, years before any aircraft could do the job. And in 1899, Wilbur and Orville Wright built a biplane kite with a wingspan of about five feet, stood in an Ohio field, and twisted its wingtips with control lines to watch it roll. That experiment became wing warping. Wing warping became the ailerons on every airliner you have ever boarded. The brothers then flew their earliest gliders at Kitty Hawk on tethers, as kites, learning the behavior of air before they were willing to hang their bodies under it. The kite has never stopped working, either. Cargo ships have been towed by computer-steered kites to cut fuel use. Kitesurfers cross open water on nothing but a canopy and a set of lines. Engineers are still trying to build kites that generate electricity by pulling a tether in loops, thousands of feet up where the wind is faster and steadier than any tower can reach. There is something worth noticing in all of this. The airplane required an engine, a century of metallurgy, and two obsessive bicycle mechanics with a homemade wind tunnel. The kite required wind, a leaf-thin sheet, and the idea of holding on. It is the cheapest flying machine ever built, it was the first, and a six year old can operate it in a park. We handed it to children anyway. That says very little about the kite. It says a great deal about how quickly we stop being impressed.
